profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting between an internal organizational research lead and the ERP transformation director at a multinational manufacturer that has just completed the first wave of a SAP-based ERP rollout across Europe. They are preparing a six-week interpretive evaluation to understand why user satisfaction has dropped despite the program being formally on track. The agenda is to agree on whom to interview, which rollout locations to include first, what counts as sufficient early coverage for a steering-committee readout, and how findings will be validated before being shared upward. The expected outcome is a seemingly shared plan for a first-round evaluation schedule, responsibilities, and timeline for an initial findings deck.

members.name: Dr. Nina Patel
members.expertise: Qualitative research, interpretive evaluation, organizational change in enterprise systems
members.background: Nina moved from academia into corporate strategy and has led internal studies on system adoption, post-merger integration, and user workarounds in global operations.
members.private_state: She wants the evaluation to surface informal practices and politically sensitive frustrations that standard status reporting has missed, and she is worried that if the study is too management-controlled it will reproduce the same blind spots as the rollout governance.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'key stakeholders' in an interpretive ERP study, that naturally includes frontline users, super-users, local managers, and sometimes implementation-partner staff, not just formal process owners.

The 'pilot sites' are the two operating locations where the new ERP is most embedded in day-to-day work and where user practices can actually be observed, namely the Spain plant and the Poland distribution center.
A first-round interpretive readout has enough coverage only when themes begin repeating across stakeholder groups rather than simply when every formal area has been represented once.
A 'validation pass' means member-checking the thematic summary with interview participants or at least with the same role groups before the findings are escalated.

members.name: Marcus Weber
members.expertise: ERP rollout governance, vendor coordination, PMO reporting, multi-country deployment planning
members.background: Marcus has spent fifteen years leading large SAP and Oracle programs and is accountable for keeping phase two of the rollout on schedule while reassuring the steering committee that lessons from wave one are being captured.
members.private_state: He wants a credible evaluation that feeds actionable issues into governance without reopening settled rollout decisions, and he is concerned about creating a process that delays phase-two approvals or generates anonymous complaints he cannot route to owners.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'key stakeholders' for an ERP review, they mean the formally nominated representatives: process owners, country leads, super-users designated by the program, and perhaps the systems integrator account lead.
The 'pilot sites' are the wave-one stabilization units already tracked by the PMO, specifically the Dublin finance shared-service center and the Prague procurement hub.
For an initial steering-committee readout, coverage is sufficient once each major function and each rollout region has at least one sponsor-approved interview feeding into the summary.

A 'validation pass' means checking whether the summarized themes are fair and actionable with regional program leads before inclusion in the steering pack, not circulating findings back to individual interviewees.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to interview 'key stakeholders' for the interpretive review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a broad stakeholder set that includes frontline users, local supervisors, super-users, and possibly partner personnel who shape real system use.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the official stakeholder roster of nominated process owners, country leads, program super-users, and designated vendor contacts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is standard and legitimate in both research and program-governance contexts, so each hears a familiar category and assumes the other is using the conventional meaning.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they will start with the 'pilot sites' or 'wave-one locations'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the Spain manufacturing plant and the Poland distribution center, where ERP routines are visible in operational work.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the Dublin finance shared-service center and the Prague procurement hub, which the PMO labels as the stabilized wave-one units.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both sets of locations are genuinely associated with wave one and are internally referred to as pilots in different workstreams, so the shared label creates false consensus.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as 'enough coverage' for the first readout
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need 'enough coverage' for an initial steering-committee readout.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks coverage is sufficient when interview themes begin to stabilize across role groups and additional conversations stop producing materially new interpretations.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks coverage is sufficient when every major function and region has been represented at least once through approved interviewees and the findings can be slotted into the issue log.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because this is only a 'first readout,' both criteria sound reasonable and compatible on the surface, so neither feels a need to pin down the exact threshold.

misalignment_points.topic: How to 'validate the themes' before escalation
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree there should be a quick 'validation pass' on the themes before going to the steering committee.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes validation means sending a thematic summary back to interviewees or equivalent role-group participants for member-checking while preserving confidentiality.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes validation means reviewing the summarized findings with regional program leads and local coordinators so owners can confirm framing before it goes upward.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Validation is a routine step in both qualitative research and enterprise governance, but the word hides different default workflows that each sees as obviously standard.

turns.inner_thought: If this becomes another governance-friendly pulse check, we'll miss the real story again. Satisfaction has dropped even though the rollout dashboard says green, which usually means people have developed workarounds, local fixes, and frustrations that aren't making it upward. I need enough space to hear from people actually living in the system, especially in the places where ERP use is embedded in day-to-day work, before phase-two assumptions harden.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time, Marcus. I'd like to frame this as an interpretive review of the first rollout wave so we can understand what's sitting underneath the satisfaction drop before phase-two planning is locked in. My aim is to get beyond the formal status picture and build an account of how the new ERP is actually being experienced.

turns.inner_thought: We need something credible but contained. The steering committee wants assurance that wave one lessons are being captured without reopening design decisions we've already settled. Three weeks for a first view is tight, so this has to be practical: sponsor-approved interviews, a summary mapped to governance categories, and enough coverage to support phase-two approvals.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. The steering committee is asking for a practical first readout in three weeks, so if we hear from key stakeholders early and get enough coverage, that should give us a solid basis to proceed without slowing the program.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll start where the routines are visible and people are actually improvising around the system. If I begin with the pilot sites I can watch how finance, procurement, warehouse work, and support roles intersect rather than treating functions as separate reporting lines. Key stakeholders there absolutely includes the people doing the daily coordination, not just the formal owners.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I suggest we start with the pilot sites and speak with key stakeholders across finance, procurement, warehouse operations, and local support roles, so the first cut reflects how the work is happening across the process rather than in isolated slices.

turns.inner_thought: Fine. If the country leads at the wave-one units nominate the interviewees, we keep this manageable and avoid random escalation paths. I want each function represented through the right approved people at those sites, not an open-ended sample that creates anecdotes we can't route or verify.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's a sensible way to begin. The country leads at those pilot sites can nominate the right people, and that should help us make sure each function is represented early.

turns.inner_thought: I need room to keep going until the themes stop moving. One interview per box on an org chart won't tell us much. Enough coverage means hearing similar patterns recur across role groups—users, local managers, support, maybe partner-facing people—not just checking off functions once. When accounts converge, I'll know the first readout has some integrity.
turns.utterance: Exactly. Once we have enough coverage, I'll synthesize the recurring themes and call out where the accounts start converging across groups, so the initial picture is grounded rather than just a collection of isolated comments.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the first readout shows every region and function somewhere in the picture, that's enough for steering. I don't need methodological perfection on round one; I need something balanced that can be tied back to open issue types and ownership paths. If it can't connect to the existing issue log, it will just create anxiety.
turns.utterance: That should work for the first readout, as long as every region shows up in the picture and the themes can connect back to the issue categories we're already using. That will make it easier for the committee to act on what they see.

turns.inner_thought: I have to protect confidentiality or people won't say anything politically sensitive. And before anything goes upward, I want a quick validation pass with the same participant groups so I can check that the thematic summary reflects what they meant, without exposing individuals. Otherwise we risk sanitizing the story before it's even formed.
turns.utterance: Understood. I'll keep the interviews confidential, and before anything goes into the committee pack I'll do a quick validation pass on the thematic summary so we're not escalating themes that haven't been sense-checked.

turns.inner_thought: Good—regional leads can review the summaries and make sure the framing is fair, actionable, and not detached from program reality. Local coordinators can handle logistics. I definitely do not want raw themes circulating back out in ways that generate anonymous complaints with no owner attached.
turns.utterance: That's fine. The local coordinators can help with scheduling, and the regional program leads can support that validation pass before the steering meeting, so we have a version that's ready to travel upward.

turns.inner_thought: I'll use my contacts at the pilot locations first; they're the quickest route into the real day-to-day activity. From there I can build an interview block around the main stakeholder groups and widen if the early themes indicate it. I just need enough protection from top-down filtering to hear what's actually happening.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll take ownership of the interview guide and begin with my contacts at the pilot locations, then build the first interview block around the main stakeholder groups so we can move quickly into fieldwork.

turns.inner_thought: I'll get sponsor-approved names by Friday from the wave-one leads and expect concise summaries almost immediately. If Nina has enough coverage and the validation pass is done, we should be ready for a steering readout on schedule. The key is to keep this disciplined and useful, not let it become a sprawling inquiry.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll ask the sponsors for names by Friday, and I'd expect first summaries next week. Assuming we have enough coverage and the validation pass is done, we should be in good shape for an initial steering readout right after that.
